target.title: Simple is as simple does: Plantinga and Ghazālī on divine simplicity
target.thesis: Most of the arguments against divine simplicity credited to Plantinga were nearly perfectly anticipated by al-Ghazālī, and his responses to Avicenna's stronger form of simplicity contain new arguments that remain valuable today.

argument.title: God cannot be a composite

atoms.A: God is a composite of more basic features
atoms.D: God is causally dependent on his distinct properties
atoms.E: God depends on properties such as power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes
atoms.F: God is simple (not a composite of more basic features)

argument.missing_premise: God is not causally dependent on his distinct properties, either efficiently or as final causes. [~D & ~E]

W4229080938.c001.text: Divine simplicity is the claim that God is not a composite of more basic features.
W4229080938.c001.quote: the notion of divine simplicity, the idea that God is not a composite of more basic features

W4229080938.c002.text: Traditional theists hold that God’s nature is absolutely simple, identical with God, so any dependence on the nature is merely self‑dependence.
W4229080938.c002.quote: God does have a nature, but that nature is absolutely simple – the property of being God, if you will – and so, the divine nature is not a composite of disparate properties out of God’s control. Moreover, God is identical with that nature, and so while God is dependent upon his nature, the dependence is an innocuous case of self‑dependence.

W4229080938.c003.text: Divine simplicity conflicts with the fact that God possesses several properties such as knowledge, power, and will.
W4229080938.c003.quote: divine simplicity flies in the face of the fact that God has several properties, such as knowledge, power, will

W4229080938.c004.text: If God is identical with a single property, then God is a property rather than a person, which is absurd.
W4229080938.c004.quote: if God is identical with that property, God is a property, not a person, which seems absurd

W4229080938.c005.text: Al‑Ghazālī’s critique of divine simplicity anticipates and exceeds Plantinga’s own criticism.
W4229080938.c005.quote: the renowned Muslim theologian Abū Ḥāmid al‑Ghazālī (d. 1111) subjects the philosophical doctrine of simplicity and the grounds for accepting it to a scathing critique, which interestingly anticipates and goes beyond Plantinga’s own critique

W4229080938.c006.text: Avicenna’s stronger version of divine simplicity can answer some of Plantinga’s objections.
W4229080938.c006.quote: Avicenna’s stronger version of divine simplicity can respond to some of Plantinga’s objections

W4229080938.c007.text: Avicenna assumes that if God had distinct properties, those properties would be parts of a whole.
W4229080938.c007.quote: the first assumption is that if God were to have distinct properties, these properties would stand to God as parts to a whole

W4229080938.c008.text: Avicenna assumes that parts taken individually differ from the whole taken collectively.
W4229080938.c008.quote: Avicenna’s second mereological assumption is that parts (or at least proper parts) taken individually are other than or different from the whole taken collectively

W4229080938.c009.text: It is contradictory for something to exist both through itself and through another.
W4229080938.c009.quote: It is simply a contradiction for something to exist both through itself and through another; it is tantamount to saying that something’s existence depends on nothing and depends on something

W4229080938.c010.text: Therefore, the Necessary Existent (God) cannot be a composite; consequently, God’s existence is simple.
W4229080938.c010.quote: Therefore, the Necessary Existent through itself, that is, God, cannot be a composite and if he is not a composite yet he exists, God’s existence is simple

W4229080938.c011.text: Traditional theists fear that a composite God would be causally dependent on his distinct properties.
W4229080938.c011.quote: for traditional theists it is fundamentally the fear that a composite God, that is, a God having distinct properties, attributes, or the like, is in some way causally dependent upon those properties

W4229080938.c012.text: If God were not simple, he would depend on properties like power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes.
W4229080938.c012.quote: if God were not simple, he would depend upon properties like power, wisdom, blessedness, in the order of final causation

W4229080938.c013.text: Plantinga argues that God possesses accidental properties that correspond to Avicennan relational properties.
W4229080938.c013.quote: Plantinga begins by first arguing that God has accidental properties, which seem to correspond to Avicennan relational properties.

W4229080938.c014.text: Avicenna holds that relational properties do not threaten divine simplicity, while Plantinga maintains that they do.
W4229080938.c014.quote: Avicenna believes that relational properties do not threaten divine simplicity, whereas Plantinga thinks that they do.

W4229080938.c015.text: Avicenna claims relational properties are not genuine properties in the sense of constitutive features.
W4229080938.c015.quote: For Avicenna, purportedly relational properties are not really properties at all, at least not in the sense of constitutive features.

W4229080938.c016.text: Plantinga asserts that possessing a given characterization makes God different from what He would have been without it.
W4229080938.c016.quote: Moreover, maintains Plantinga, possessing a given characterization does make God ‘different from what he would have been had it not characterized him’.

W4229080938.c017.text: Medieval philosophers agree that God’s many actions can be traced to Him, but these effects need not arise from distinct essential properties or characterizations.
W4229080938.c017.quote: Both sides in the medieval debate agreed that God’s ultimately numerous different actions or effects can be traced back to God; however, they also insisted that those different effects of his action need not emanate from different essential properties or even necessarily from different ways of characterizing God.

W4229080938.c018.text: The shift from properties to characteristics does not indicate real differences within the divinity.
W4229080938.c018.quote: Thus, Plantinga’s shift from properties to characteristics need not show that there are real differences within the divinity.

W4229080938.c019.text: Avicenna argues that God’s knowledge of a thing is the ultimate cause of that thing’s existence, so knowing and creating are identical in God.
W4229080938.c019.quote: Avicenna anticipates Plantinga’s own examples of creating and knowing, and explicitly argues that God’s knowledge of a thing is the ultimate cause of that thing’s existence. In other words, according to Avicenna for God to know the world, which includes Adam, is for God to create the world, which includes Adam.

W4229080938.c020.text: According to the traditional view, God lacks all potentiality and is fully actual, unlike humans whose knowing is a potentiality.
W4229080938.c020.quote: In the case of humans, knowing is a type of potentiality we have, whereas on the traditional view of God, God is devoid of all potentiality and instead God is fully actual.

W4229080938.c021.text: Plantinga challenges the claim that God has no potential properties, asserting that God later acquires such properties.
W4229080938.c021.quote: He challenges the claim that God has no potential properties, which he subsequently acquires.

W4229080938.c022.text: Plantinga’s intuition is that it seems right to think God lacks characteristics he could have had but may acquire.
W4229080938.c022.quote: The reason he gives for holding his preferred position is ‘it seems right to think that there are characteristics [God] lacks but could have had. It is natural to think, furthermore, that among these there are some he hasn’t yet acquired but could acquire’ (Plantinga (1980), 44).

W4229080938.c023.text: Plantinga defines a potential property as one that God lacks at some time t1 and possesses at a later time t2.
W4229080938.c023.quote: Given Plantinga’s subsequent challenge to the traditionalists’ assumption about God’s relation to time, at least in Does God Have a Nature, he seems to understand ‘potential property’ in terms of temporal frequency: x has some potential property, P, just in case there is a time t1 when x does not possess P, and then some subsequent time t2 when x does possess P.

W4229080938.c024.text: Ghazali maintains that all of God’s relational properties involve volition, which requires choosing among possible options.
W4229080938.c024.quote: Ghazālī insists that all of God’s relational properties involve God’s volition, and that volition must involve choosing among different possible options.

W4229080938.c025.text: Ghazali and other theologians object that Avicenna’s notion of volition makes God compelled and not truly sovereign.
W4229080938.c025.quote: It certainly did for Ghazālī and other theologians, who thought it so eviscerated the notion of will as to make God compelled, even if by his nature, and so not truly sovereign.

W4229080938.c026.text: The view Ghazali opposes holds that if God were not simple, He would be causally dependent on parts, threatening His aseity.
W4229080938.c026.quote: God purportedly must be simple, otherwise he is causally dependent upon his parts by way of material causality, and so his aseity is challenged.

W4229080938.c027.text: Ghazālī recasts God’s relation to attributes as a self and its attributes rather than as a whole constituted by parts.
W4229080938.c027.quote: First, he recasts the description of God’s relation to his attributes or properties in terms of a self and attributes that characterize that self rather than in terms of a whole constituted by its parts.

W4229080938.c028.text: Ghazālī questions whether the Aristotelian notion of material causation is a genuine form of causation or merely a technical term.
W4229080938.c028.quote: Second, he questions whether the Aristotelian notion of material causation is a genuine form of causation or just a term of art.

W4229080938.c029.text: Ghazālī advises abandoning the description of God as the Necessary Existent through itself, emphasizing instead that God is the eternally uncaused cause of everything.
W4229080938.c029.quote: Third, he counsels doing away with describing God as the Necessary Existent through itself, since the most important description is that the divine is the eternally uncaused cause of everything else.

W4229080938.c030.text: The relation between the divine self and its attributes is a grounding relation, not a causal relation.
W4229080938.c030.quote: In effect, as we shall see, Ghazālī suggests that the relation between the divine self and its attributes is a grounding relation rather than a causal relation.

W4229080938.c031.text: An efficient cause requires the cause to be extrinsic to its effect and the effect to derive its existence from the cause; the divine self and attributes are not extrinsic, so no efficient cause exists.
W4229080938.c031.quote: Here presumably Ghazālī intends Avicenna’s own account of an efficient cause: x is an efficient cause of y just in case (1) x is extrinsic to y and (2) y has its existence from x.

W4229080938.c032.text: If God needs anything for his existence or perfection, then he is not absolutely self‑sufficient, jeopardizing his aseity.
W4229080938.c032.quote: Thus, one might object that given that God is the Necessary Existent through itself, God cannot need anything for his existence and perfection. If God needs anything, then he is not absolutely self‑sufficient...

W4229080938.c033.text: If God is identical with each of his properties, then God has only one property, contradicting the fact that God possesses several distinct properties.
W4229080938.c033.quote: Plantinga identifies the ‘substantial’ difficulty as this: ‘If God is identical with each of his properties, then each of his properties is identical with each of his properties, so that God has but one property. This seems flatly incompatible with the obvious fact that God has several properties’.

W4229080938.c034.text: Ghazālī notes that different divine attributes have distinct accounts, meanings, or senses, so they are not all the same.
W4229080938.c034.quote: Such attributions as existing necessarily, knowing, willing, etc. all have different accounts, meanings, or senses (maʿānin) observes Ghazālī.

W4229080938.c035.text: Ghazālī fully agrees with this objection, confirming the problem.

W4229080938.c036.text: Asserting that God knows things other than himself entails abandoning divine simplicity.
W4229080938.c036.quote: If, conversely, one asserts that God knows things other than himself, as Avicenna did, then, claims Ghazālī, one implicitly has given up divine simplicity.

W4229080938.c037.text: The knowledge of oneself is distinct from the knowledge of another.
W4229080938.c037.quote: That is because the knowledge of oneself is distinct and different from the knowledge of another.

W4229080938.c038.text: Within God there are at least two distinct entities: his knowledge of himself and his knowledge of the world.
W4229080938.c038.quote: Consequently, within God there are at least two distinct things, namely, his knowledge of himself and additionally his knowledge of the other, that is, the world.

W4229080938.c039.text: Avicenna claimed that God’s knowledge of others is identical with his knowledge of himself.
W4229080938.c039.quote: Avicenna had attempted to avoid this conclusion by saying that God’s knowledge of others is identical with his knowledge of himself.

W4229080938.c040.text: Causation involves a relation (iḍāfa) between cause and effect.
W4229080938.c040.quote: Causation involves a relation (iḍāfa), namely, between the cause and the effect.

W4229080938.c041.text: If God knows that he is causing, then there must be multiplicity in divine knowledge.
W4229080938.c041.quote: Consequently, if God knows that he is causing – and recall that Avicenna’s own account of divine volition required that God does know that he is acting – and God’s causing is different from God, as Ghazālī believes he has shown, there must be multiplicity in the divine knowledge.

W4229080938.c042.text: Divine simplicity is incompatible with God’s omniscience.
W4229080938.c042.quote: In short, concludes Ghazālī, divine simplicity is incompatible with God’s omniscience.

W4229080938.c043.text: When forced to choose, omniscience is clearly required for God, while simplicity is not obviously required.
W4229080938.c043.quote: If one must decide between the two, the decision is obvious: anything worthy of the title God must be omniscient, whereas it is not at all obvious that it must be simple.

W4229080938.c044.text: The remaining problem is to determine the relation between God’s essential properties and his aseity and sovereignty if God is not absolutely simple.
W4229080938.c044.quote: the initial problems for which simplicity was put forth still remain: what is the relation between God’s essential properties and his aseity and sovereignty, if God is not absolutely simple?

W4229080938.c045.text: Ghazālī illustrates the distinction between the divine self and its causal relation by asking us to imagine ourselves being caused.
W4229080938.c045.quote: Ghazālī further motivates this distinction between the divine self and its causal relation to the world by having us imagine ourselves and our being caused, and so being related to another.

W4229080938.c046.text: It is possible for a being to know itself without also knowing any other entity.
W4229080938.c046.quote: He notes that it is possible for one to know oneself without also knowing any other, and so not knowing one’s relation of being caused.

W4229080938.c047.text: It is impossible, indeed contradictory, for a being to know itself without also knowing itself.
W4229080938.c047.quote: In contrast, it is impossible, indeed a contradiction, for one to know oneself without also knowing oneself.

W4229080938.c048.text: Since the possible differs from the impossible, knowledge of the self and knowledge of the self’s relation to another must be different.
W4229080938.c048.quote: Now the possible is different from the impossible, and so knowledge of the self and knowledge of the self’s relation to another must be different.

W4229080938.c049.text: For God to know himself and the causal relation he must have at least two distinct kinds of knowledge.
W4229080938.c049.quote: Thus, for God to know himself, that is, one of the relata, and to know that this causal relation exists again requires that within God there are at least two distinct things, namely, God’s knowledge of himself and additionally his knowledge of this causal relation.

W4229080938.c050.text: Frank’s advice to translate dhāt as “entity” or a pronoun is wise because medieval Muslim thinkers treat dhāt as a bearer of properties, not as a property itself.
W4229080938.c050.quote: Frank’s advice is sage particularly when presenting medieval Islamicate thought to contemporary analytic philosophers, where an essence is usually understood as a necessary and unique property (cf. Plantinga (2003), 78–79, 140), whereas for our medieval Muslim thinkers dhāt is decidedly not a property but the bearer of properties.

W4229080938.c051.text: The reason medieval theologians and philosophers give for God being essentially outside time is that time belongs to the created order.
W4229080938.c051.quote: One reason put forth by both theologians and philosophers alike for thinking that God must essentially be outside time is that time itself is part of the created order.

W4229080938.c052.text: Therefore, because God is independent of creation, God must be outside time or can exist when there is no time.
W4229080938.c052.quote: Consequently, God considered independent of creation, must be outside of time, or at the very least God can/does exist when there is no time.

W4229080938.c053.text: Plantinga could explain God’s accidental properties via possible worlds, but in On Does God Have a Nature he instead relies only on temporal properties.
W4229080938.c053.quote: Thus, while God as a necessary being would exist in every possible world, God’s accidental properties would be different contingent upon which world book characterizes a given possible world. Still, in On Does God Have a Nature, Plantilla does not avail himself of these sources, and instead appeals exclusively to properties that God is yet to have, now has or will have, all temporal indicators.

W4229080938.c054.text: Ghazālī anticipates the modal collapse argument, which claims that divine simplicity implies that everything exists necessarily.
W4229080938.c054.quote: At Ghazālī (2000b), discussion 3, he raises his concerns, which almost exactly anticipate the so-called ‘modal collapse argument’, which purports to show that divine simplicity entails that everything exists necessarily.

W4229080938.c055.text: Tomaszewski and Schmid argue that the modal collapse argument is invalid because it makes an improper substitution in a modal context.
W4229080938.c055.quote: Recently, Christopher Tomaszewski (2019), followed by Joseph Schmid (2022), have questioned the logical validity of the argument, claiming that it involves an invalid substitution into a modal context.

W4229080938.c056.text: Ghazālī’s shift in language may beg the question against Avicenna’s position.
W4229080938.c056.quote: While Ghazālī’s shift in language does give him a rhetorical advantage, it also potentially begs the question against Avicenna.

W4229080938.c057.text: Avicenna maintains that there is a single self or entity (dhāt) that is free of any dependence except possibly self‑dependence.
W4229080938.c057.quote: Avicenna’s aim is to show that there is one self or entity (dhāt) that is free of any dependence, other than perhaps the trivial property of self‑dependence.

W4229080938.c058.text: If God is a composite of a self and attributes, a cause is needed to compose them, which would function as an efficient cause.
W4229080938.c058.quote: One might argue that if God is a composite of a self and attributes, then there must be a cause that provides composition to the divine self and its attributes, and so explains God’s unity as well as all of God’s attributes’ acting in a unified way.

W4229080938.c059.text: Ghazālī argues that modal notions should be treated as de dicto propositions and need not be grounded in existent things.
W4229080938.c059.quote: It is worth noting that unlike Avicenna who was a modal realist and believed that there are things in the world that have de re possibilities and necessities, Ghazālī, at least in the Incoherence, suggests that modal notions should be understood in terms of de dicto propositions and as such need not be grounded in existents in the world; see Ghazālī (2000b) discussion 1 [116–119].

W4229080938.c060.text: For Ghazālī, saying “God is necessary” is incoherent because no proposition about God exists for the modal operator to apply to.
W4229080938.c060.quote: Consequently, for Ghazālī, while one can say, ‘“God exists eternally” is necessary’ or ‘“God does not have an efficient cause” is necessary’, to say, ‘God is necessary’ would be for him ill‑formed at best and simply incoherent at worse, since in the latter case, there is no proposition about God over which the modal operator ranges.

W4229080938.c061.text: Ghazālī’s shift from describing God as the Necessary through itself to calling God eternal and uncaused is explained by his concern that attributing necessity to God is incoherent.
W4229080938.c061.quote: Such a concern would again explain Ghazālī’s shift from the Avicennan language of describing God as the Necessary through itself, to Ghazālī’s own preferred language of the eternal and uncauses.

W4229080938.c062.text: A concern about the ranges of the modal operator explains Ghazālī’s shift from describing God as the Necessary through itself to describing God as eternal and uncaused.
W4229080938.c062.quote: Such a concern would again explain Ghazālī’s shift from the Avicennan language of describing God as the Necessary through itself, to Ghazālī’s own preferred language of the eternal and uncauses.

W4229080938.c063.text: Ghazālī changed his theological language from the Avicennan description of God as the Necessary through itself to his own description of God as eternal and uncaused.
W4229080938.c063.quote: Ghazālī’s shift from the Avicennan language of describing God as the Necessary through itself, to Ghazālī’s own preferred language of the eternal and uncauses.

W4229080938.c064.text: An anonymous referee suggested a similar point but attributed to Ghazālī a temporal‑frequency modal of modalities.
W4229080938.c064.quote: I am grateful to an anonymous referee for suggesting a similar point, albeit they ascribed to Ghazālī a temporal frequency modal of modalities.

W4229080938.arg1.mp.text: God is not causally dependent on his distinct properties, either efficiently or as final causes.

W4229080938.arg2.mp.text: God's omniscience requires that he know things other than himself.

W4229080938.a1.text: Most arguments against divine simplicity attributed to Plantinga were anticipated by al‑Ghazālī.
W4229080938.a1.quote: most of the argumentation against divine simplicity frequently credited to Plantinga had been nearly perfectly anticipated by al‑Ghazālī.

W4229080938.a2.text: Ghazālī’s new arguments remain valuable and informative for today’s discussion of divine simplicity.
W4229080938.a2.quote: Ghazālī develops ‘new’ arguments and moves that are still valuable and informative to the discussion of divine simplicity today.

W4229080938.arg1.r1.text: God is not a composite of any features on which his existence or activity depends, whether those features are ordered by priority or co-equal.

W4229080938.arg1.r2.text: If God were composite, his unity would be grounded in distinct constituents on which his existence depends, a dependence not removed by treating those constituents as modes of a single act.

W4229080938.arg1.r3.text: If God were composite, his unity would be grounded in distinct constituents (the properties he exemplifies) on which his existence depends, whether efficiently or in grounding, so that a necessary existent that is not simple depends on what it is not.

objections.text: Consider a being G with two distinct features: power P and wisdom W, with G composite. Suppose G's final cause is the good of exercising P and W together, so G is directed toward a state of affairs that includes both. Now stipulate that P and W are not standing sources that G consults; they are modes of G's own activity, individuated only by what G does. Mapping this onto c012: 'if G were not simple, G would depend on P, W as final causes' requires that each feature be an independent target G must aim at. But here G's end is an activity G itself performs, and the features are specifications of that activity, not external goals. Any composite whose parts are grounded in its own activity can have a final cause that is the whole, so no part is a final cause that G depends on in the sense the antecedent needs. The conditional's consequent fails: composition does not entail dependence on distinct final causes, because the final cause can be the composite's own unified act rather than its constituents.
objections.premise_fails_because: c012 fails because it assumes that non-simplicity forces each distinct property to be a separate final cause G depends on, when a composite whose features are modes of one self-directed activity can have a single unified final cause that is not any of its distinct properties.

objections.text: W4229080938.c001 defines divine simplicity as God not being a composite of more basic features. The argument then infers that if God depended on distinct properties like power or wisdom, he would be composite and therefore not simple. But properties such as wisdom are not "more basic features" that compose a substance the way parts make up a whole; they are attributes had by it. The premise assumes without justification that having distinct properties is the same as being built out of parts. This is a scope shift: c001 concerns composition by parts, whereas the argument needs properties to function as composing parts to reach its conclusion. Without a missing step showing that instantiating distinct properties just is being composed of more basic features, c001 cannot bridge causal dependence on properties to divine simplicity.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4229080938.c001 fails because it defines simplicity as the absence of part-whole composition, yet the argument treats distinct properties as if they were composing parts, which leaves a missing step between instantiating properties and being a composite of more basic features.

objections.text: Consider an equilateral triangle. It has distinct properties—equilaterality, equiangularity, and three-sidedness—yet none of these is more basic than the others or than the triangle itself. They are co-fundamental aspects of one nature. The triangle is therefore not a composite of more basic features, but it plainly has distinct properties. Now apply this to the premise: 'not a composite of more basic features' is compatible with having distinct properties that are co-equal aspects of a single nature. But the whole point of divine simplicity, as the surrounding premises reveal, is to rule out distinct properties on which God might depend. The definition in c001 fails because non-composition from more basic features does not exclude distinct properties. A God whose power, wisdom, and blessedness were co-fundamental aspects of his one nature—none more basic, none composing him from parts—would satisfy c001's definition yet still have the distinct properties c011 and c012 treat as threatening. The premise misdefines divine simplicity in a way that is too weak to do the work the argument requires.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4229080938.c001 fails because defining divine simplicity as non-composition from more basic features does not exclude having distinct co-fundamental properties, which is exactly what the argument needs to rule out.

objections.text: In metallurgy, alloys gain strength precisely because their composite parts interact; the whole depends on its constituents, yet this dependence does not diminish the alloy’s unity or integrity. If a being’s properties were like alloy components—each reinforcing the others—then causal reliance on them would not imply fragility or contingency. The fear assumes dependence entails weakness, but interdependence can instead create stability.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4229080938.c011 fails because dependence on parts does not necessarily undermine unity or self-sufficiency.

objections.text: c001 defines divine simplicity as God not being a composite of 'more basic features.' This smuggles in a hierarchical assumption: that any genuine composition requires parts strictly ontologically prior to the whole. But c011 and c012 describe the actual threat—God depending on power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes. These are not 'more basic' than God; they are co-equal attributes or modes at the same ontological level. A composite of co-equal features (a whole constituted by aspects none of which is 'more basic' than the others) is excluded by c001's definition yet is precisely the structure c012 fears. The argument needs c001 to rule out that structure, but c001's 'more basic' qualifier makes it incapable of doing so. The premise assumes a part-whole hierarchy the rest of the argument never establishes and that the causal-dependence worry does not require.

The Being is the locus of these properties, but the properties exist independently of the Being. The existence of a plurality of real, instantiated properties does not imply that the being is directed toward those properties for its own completion or that they act as its final cause. objections.text: An ontological realist holds that properties such as wisdom and power are distinct, irreducible entities. If God possesses these properties, he is necessarily a composite being made up of these separate components. Consequently, God's identity is determined by the combination of these properties, making him dependent on them.

objections.text: Imagine a cosmic guardian named Aeon that exists necessarily. Aeon has two co-equal aspects: Sight, by which it perceives all worlds, and Reach, by which it sustains them. These are not separable parts; they are distinct, mutually grounding features of Aeon's single substance. Aeon's existence and activity plainly depend on both: without Sight, Aeon could not know; without Reach, Aeon could not act. Yet Sight and Reach are not something other than Aeon—they are Aeon itself, formally distinguished. Aeon depends on them the way a flame depends on its heat and light: not as external causes, but as internal determinations of its own nature. Thus Aeon is a composite of co-equal features on which its existence and activity depend, yet it exists through itself and not through another.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise arg1.r1 fails because it wrongly assumes that any composition involving dependence on distinct features entails dependence on an external other, whereas a single substance can depend on its own formally distinct aspects.

objections.text: In a kiln, a single glass goblet exists. It has distinct constituents: translucency, fragility, and a stemmed shape. These are not independent parts bolted together; they are modes of one continuous act of glass-existing. The goblet does not exist through translucency as a final cause and again through fragility as another. Were fragility a separate constituent, the goblet might depend on it; but fragility is simply how this glass behaves under stress. Shatter the glass and the goblet ceases, yet fragility is not a constituent on which the goblet relies like a wheel on an axle; it is the goblet’s own act under a different description. Treating its distinct features as modes of a single act removes the causal dependence that composition would otherwise impose.

objections.text: Imagine a necessary existent, the Nexus, whose essence includes three co-necessary properties: creative power, perfect knowledge, and perfect goodness. Each property is individually necessary—none could fail to obtain in any possible world—and they mutually entail one another, so that power without knowledge would not be the Nexus's power, knowledge without goodness would not be the Nexus's knowledge, and so on. The Nexus is composite: it has genuinely distinct features. Yet the Nexus does not depend on 'what it is not.' Each property is part of what the Nexus IS, not an external constituent on which it leans. The properties are not prior to the Nexus; they are co-constitutive aspects of a single necessary nature. The Nexus's unity is not grounded in something other than itself; it is grounded in its own essentially multi-featured nature. Composition here is internal structure, not dependence on an alien ground.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection engages directly with c001 as stated. It takes the definition of divine simplicity as 'not a composite of more basic features' at face value and argues that the qualifier 'more basic' creates a gap: the causal-dependence worry in c012 involves co-equal attributes, not ontologically prior parts, so c001's wording cannot rule out the very structure the argument fears. rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that c001's 'more basic' wording is too narrow, and I will not defend it as written. The argument's real target, as c011 and c012 show, is dependence: a God who is a whole of power, wisdom and blessedness would have those features as final causes for his existence and activity, and that is what the simplicity claim is meant to block. Co-equal aspects can ground dependence just as well as ordered parts can, so the definition should say that God is not composed of features on which his existence depends, whether or not those features are ordered. The 'more basic' qualifier smuggles in a part-whole priority the argument never needs. Literature supports reading simplicity as ruling out composition in general rather than only hierarchical composition [W4232242998.a1], and [W2086535520.a1] describes simplicity as lacking any composition or metaphysical complexity, which is broader than the priority reading. The mp premise, that God is not causally dependent on his distinct properties either efficiently or as final causes, is unchanged. The revised c001 is what needs to change: it must name the dependence relation, not priority, as the thing excluded.

Revised premise: God is not a composite of any features on which his existence or activity depends, whether those features are ordered by priority or co-equal.

You are right that c001 is too narrow as it stands. The phrase 'more basic features' suggests a hierarchical part-whole relation, but the causal-dependence worry in c012 applies to any composition of distinct features, whether or not they are ranked as prior to the whole. In the broader tradition, divine simplicity is intended to rule out any composition in God whatsoever [W4232242998.a1], and the thesis is standardly understood as the denial of all proper parts, composition, or metaphysical complexity [W2086535520.a1]. Ghazālī recasts God's relation to attributes as a self and its attributes rather than as a whole constituted by parts [W4229080938.c027], and the classical view insists that divine attributes do not pick out distinct parts [W7172336769.c016]. The causal argument in c009, c011, and c012 targets dependence on distinct properties as final causes, and that threat remains even if the properties are co-equal modes. So the argument survives only if we drop the limiting qualifier. I concede that c001 must be revised.

It offers a counterexample in which a composite being's final cause is its own unified activity rather than its constituent properties, arguing that composition does not entail dependence on distinct properties as final causes. rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
The objection pins the consequent of c012 on the claim that each feature is an independent target G must aim at. That is more than the argument needs. c011 frames the worry as dependence on distinct properties, and the relevant dependence is ontological: a composite's unity is secured by its constituents, so its existence and its end are answerable to them. Your proposal that G's end is a unified act whose specifications are P and W does not dissolve this. If P and W are individuated only by what G does, then they are determinations of one act, and the act is what G depends on for its specification. That is still dependence on distinct items, now as formal rather than external final causes. The sense in which the argument needs the consequent is exactly the sense in which Plantinga and Ghazālī's discussion treats attributes as not extrinsic to the divine self [W4229080938.c031], and whether the act-individuation picture escapes this turns on whether the act is prior to its specifications. Ockham's worry that distinct attributes would remain distinct without activity [W2003018038.a2] suggests that the specifications carry their own distinctness, which is the feature the argument targets. I concede that the bare conditional, read as requiring independent external goals, is too strong and should be restated. The revised premise is that if God were composite, his unity would be grounded in distinct constituents that his existence depends on in the sense that cannot be removed by reconstruing them as modes of one act.

Revised premise: If God were composite, his unity would be grounded in distinct constituents on which his existence depends, a dependence not removed by treating those constituents as modes of a single act.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W4229080938.c012 as stated. That premise claims that if God were not simple, he would depend on properties like power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes. The objection provides a countermodel: a being that instantiates distinct, independent universals (Justice and Wisdom) without those properties functioning as final causes or sources of causal dependence. This is a direct assault on the conditional claim in c012, arguing that non-simplicity does not entail final-causal dependence. Whether the countermodel is persuasive or not, the objection engages the premise as written rather than attributing to the argument a claim it does not make.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that instantiating independent universals does not by itself make a being causally dependent on them, and the argument should not claim that it does. Plantinga-style defenders of simplicity have always separated being many-featured from depending on the features [W4229080938.c011]. But the argument's real claim is narrower: a composite God would have his existence or activity depend on constituents, whether efficiently or as final causes [W4229080938.c012]. Your Platonist picture has the Being exemplify Justice and Wisdom, and the objection says the Being is not directed toward them for its completion. That concedes the relevant point only if the Being's existence and activity are independent of its exemplifying them. On the Platonic model, though, the Being is the locus that is just and wise; its being just is a way it is, and a Necessary Existent whose unity is grounded in exemplifying distinct universals depends on those universals for being the unified thing it is. That is the grounding dependence r2 names, and treating the constituents as modes of a single act does not remove it. The objection therefore leaves r2 untouched rather than refuting c012. The objection does show that c012 is too quick, since final causation is not the only route to dependence, but it does not show that the composite God escapes dependence.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You conflate the description of a being with its constitution. Even if the Being’s identity is characterized by its exemplification of distinct universals, this "grounding" of unity is merely the relation of instantiation. To say a being's unity is "grounded" in its properties is to say the Being is the single subject of those properties. This does not make the Being a composite of those properties, nor does it imply it depends on them for its existence. If the Being is the necessary locus for these eternal universals, the "grounding" you describe is simply the ontological way those properties are realized in a single subject. You have not demonstrated that being many-featured necessitates being a composite, nor that the relation of instantiation constitutes the kind of dependence that undermines simplicity.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that c012, read as a claim about final causes alone, is too narrow, and I concede that much. Being many-featured through instantiation of independent universals does not by itself make a being depend on them as final causes [W4229080938.c011]. But your rejoinder gives me the premise I need. You say the Being is the single subject of its properties, and that unity is merely instantiation. Granted. Then the Being's being one thing that is just and wise is the same as its standing in the instantiation relation to two distinct universals. If the Being's unity is nothing over and above those relata, the Being is a composite in the sense the argument needs: its unity is grounded in distinct constituents. Whether that grounding is dependence in the existence-sense r2 requires is the open question. Simplicity's traditional opponents would press that the Necessary Existent would then exist only given the universals' standing as its constituents, which conflicts with aseity [W3115675310.c029]. You have not shown that instantiation is non-dependent in that sense, and you have not shown that the Being's existence is independent of the universals it instantiates. So I do not concede the r2 dependence. I do concede that c012 as stated, about final causes, is not the right premise, and the argument should be restated around grounding of unity.

Revised premise: If God were composite, his unity would be grounded in distinct constituents (the properties he exemplifies) on which his existence depends, whether efficiently or in grounding, so that a necessary existent that is not simple depends on what it is not.

That said, your case exposes that [W4229080938.c012] overreaches by specifying final causes, since Platonic instantiation is not teleological dependence. The objection provides a concrete counterexample—City X—arguing that a thing can exist through a self-grounded fact and through another fact without incoherence, using truthmaker theory to show multiple co-existent grounds for a single truth. Whether or not this counterexample is compelling or uses the same notion of 'through' the argument intends, the objection is engaging the premise as written rather than attacking a claim the argument does not make.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: The City X case is instructive, but it targets the wrong relation. Co-existent truthmakers for 'City X exists' do not show that the city exists through itself and through another in the sense c009 needs. The city's existence is a single fact about the city; the two truthmakers are two grounds for one proposition, and the charter does not make the city's existence depend on the street arrangement in the way divine existence would have to depend on a composite. c009 is about the thing's own existence being derived from something else, and the City X case concedes that the city is contingent on both, so it is not a case of a Necessary Existent. The argument's own revised premise r2 locates the problem in dependence of God's existence on distinct constituents, and that dependence is not removed by saying the constituents are truthmakers. Truthmaker pluralism therefore answers a question about propositions, while the argument asks about the metaphysics of a being's existence. On the truthmaker side, the literature offers a route that favours the argument: God can be the truthmaker for divine predicates without property exemplification [W7172336769.c066], and grounding of 'God is good' in God's being rather than an added predicate [W7172336769.c072]. That makes the grounding single rather than plural, which is what c009 requires. I accept that c009 as worded ('something exist both through itself and through another') is too loose; the claim should be restricted to necessary existence grounded in distinct sources. That restriction is the revision I propose.
rounds.revised_premise: It is contradictory for a Necessary Existent to have its existence grounded both in itself and in some distinct fact or constituent on which it depends.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: Defender, your reply sidesteps the point that truth‑maker pluralism does not hinge on contingency. Nothing in the theory rules out a necessary existent having several co‑existent grounds – the grounds need not be contingent, they only need to be distinct. If God’s existence were grounded in a property‑type “power” and a distinct property‑type “wisdom,” each could serve as an independent truth‑maker for the proposition “God exists” without rendering God contingent. Your move to restrict c009 to “necessary existence grounded in distinct sources” simply re‑labels the issue; it does not show that such distinct sources cannot both ground a necessary being. Moreover, the claim that treating the constituents as “modes of a single act” removes dependence is precisely what the pluralist truth‑maker picture denies: the modes remain separate grounds even if they are unified in a single act. Hence your revision leaves the core objection untouched.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that truthmaker pluralism does not require contingency, and I withdraw the contingency restriction I offered before: distinct grounds could in principle both ground a necessary being. But the pluralist picture only generates the contradiction c009 asserts if each truthmaker is an independent ground of the thing's existence, and that is exactly what r2 denies to matter. The argument's core claim is not that a necessary being cannot have several truthmakers for a proposition, but that God's existence cannot depend on distinct constituents. Your modes point is the decisive one: if the modes remain separate grounds, then God's existence depends on them and r2 applies, so the objection lands on r2, not on a mere relabelling. I cannot rescue the argument by appeal to a single grounding relation without the premise doing the work, and the literature I cited ([W7172336769.c066], [W7172336769.c072]) supplies truthmaker grounding in God's being, not in distinct grounds, so it supports a single-ground reading, not the plural one the objection targets. Where I stand: c009 as worded does not survive, because the City X case shows that co-existent truthmakers are coherent. The argument survives only if it is restated so that its contradiction premise concerns dependence of existence on distinct constituents, which is what r2 already asserts. That restated premise is the one that must carry the weight.

Revised premise: It is contradictory for a necessary being's existence to be grounded in distinct constituents on which that existence depends, so that a necessary existent must have a single, non-plural ground for its existence.

City X is contingent and not self-grounded; its charter and layout are merely plural truthmakers for a proposition, not ontological constituents on which the city’s existence causally depends. The revised premises make clear that the worry is about a necessary being depending for existence or unity on distinct features. Truthmaker theory actually aids the simple theist: God Himself can be the sole truthmaker for divine predicates without distinct property exemplifications [W7172336769.c066], because ‘God is good’ is true in virtue of God’s being, not an added intrinsic predicate [W7172336769.c072]. Your example thus does not show that a necessary being can exist both through itself and through another; it shows only that contingent truths can have plural truthmakers, which the argument never denied. rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that c001 as written does not carry the inference. The word 'composite' there invites the parts-whole reading you describe, and the argument never supplied the bridge. The revised premises already move away from that wording: r1 defines simplicity as God not being composed of features on which his existence or activity depends, whether ordered or co-equal, and r3 locates the composition in the exemplified properties on which existence depends. That shift is what the argument needs, and it is the place where your objection bites. Your strongest rival is that properties are not distinct items at all: God has no properties, everything he is is one pure act [W7172336769.c014], and abstract names signify the one divine being under different aspects [W7172336769.c029]. If that is right, c012's dependence is on the one being, not on distinct constituents, and the argument has no composition to derive. The argument can answer only by denying that aspect-talk removes the dependence, which is the claim in r2, and that claim needs support I have not yet given. So the argument survives only with c001 replaced and with the bridge made explicit.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: You treat "composite of more basic features" as mereological composition, but the argument does not restrict "features" to physical parts. It relies on the Avicennian framework where distinct properties function as parts or constituents of a whole [W4229080938.c007], and the classical simplicity tradition explicitly denies that God has distinct metaphysical parts, properties, or constituents [W2013411601.a1][W1550130099.a1]. On this metaphysics, a necessary being's distinct properties are not external accidents but internal constituents that ground its unity and existence, so c001 already targets metaphysical composition by properties, not just physical parts. The argument does not assume without justification that having distinct properties is being built out of parts; indeed, classical simplicity denies that God "has" properties in the first place [W7172336769.c014]. The scope shift you allege disappears once we recognize that "features" in this tradition refers to any metaphysical constituents, including properties [W2013411601.a1].

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You reinterpret “features” as metaphysical constituents, but you did not answer my point about *more basic*. c001 says God is not a composite of *more basic* features. Yet the distinct properties you cite—power, wisdom—are standardly posterior to the substance that bears them, not prior constituents on which it depends for its existence. Unless you supply a premise showing that these properties are ontologically prior to God and genuinely compose him, you cannot derive a violation of c001 from the mere claim that God would depend on them. The scope shift therefore survives: you are using “composite of more basic features” to cover dependence on posterior perfections, and the crucial step linking distinct properties to prior, grounding constituents remains missing.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right to press on 'more basic.' In Aristotelian metaphysics, properties like wisdom are typically posterior to the substance that bears them, so the argument cannot simply assume that distinct properties are more basic than God merely because he would depend on them. While the classical tradition does treat distinct properties as metaphysical constituents or parts [W2013411601.a1][W4229080938.c007], the inference from dependence to composition of *more basic* features requires a step the argument lacks: showing that these constituents are prior to, not posterior to, the divine substance. I concede that this gap is real. The argument would be better served by dropping the priority qualifier from c001 and targeting dependence on distinct constituents directly, as the classical denial of distinct metaphysical parts, properties, or constituents already suggests [W2013411601.a1].

objection.text: Consider a being G with two distinct features: power P and wisdom W, with G composite. Suppose G's final cause is the good of exercising P and W together, so G is directed toward a state of affairs that includes both. Now stipulate that P and W are not standing sources that G consults; they are modes of G's own activity, individuated only by what G does. Mapping this onto c012: 'if G were not simple, G would depend on P, W as final causes' requires that each feature be an independent target G must aim at. But here G's end is an activity G itself performs, and the features are specifications of that activity, not external goals. Any composite whose parts are grounded in its own activity can have a final cause that is the whole, so no part is a final cause that G depends on in the sense the antecedent needs. The conditional's consequent fails: composition does not entail dependence on distinct final causes, because the final cause can be the composite's own unified act rather than its constituents.
objection.premise_fails_because: c012 fails because it assumes that non-simplicity forces each distinct property to be a separate final cause G depends on, when a composite whose features are modes of one self-directed activity can have a single unified final cause that is not any of its distinct properties.

objection.text: W4229080938.c001 defines divine simplicity as God not being a composite of more basic features. The argument then infers that if God depended on distinct properties like power or wisdom, he would be composite and therefore not simple. But properties such as wisdom are not "more basic features" that compose a substance the way parts make up a whole; they are attributes had by it. The premise assumes without justification that having distinct properties is the same as being built out of parts. This is a scope shift: c001 concerns composition by parts, whereas the argument needs properties to function as composing parts to reach its conclusion. Without a missing step showing that instantiating distinct properties just is being composed of more basic features, c001 cannot bridge causal dependence on properties to divine simplicity.
objection.premise_fails_because: W4229080938.c001 fails because it defines simplicity as the absence of part-whole composition, yet the argument treats distinct properties as if they were composing parts, which leaves a missing step between instantiating properties and being a composite of more basic features.

objection.text: Consider an equilateral triangle. It has distinct properties—equilaterality, equiangularity, and three-sidedness—yet none of these is more basic than the others or than the triangle itself. They are co-fundamental aspects of one nature. The triangle is therefore not a composite of more basic features, but it plainly has distinct properties. Now apply this to the premise: 'not a composite of more basic features' is compatible with having distinct properties that are co-equal aspects of a single nature. But the whole point of divine simplicity, as the surrounding premises reveal, is to rule out distinct properties on which God might depend. The definition in c001 fails because non-composition from more basic features does not exclude distinct properties. A God whose power, wisdom, and blessedness were co-fundamental aspects of his one nature—none more basic, none composing him from parts—would satisfy c001's definition yet still have the distinct properties c011 and c012 treat as threatening. The premise misdefines divine simplicity in a way that is too weak to do the work the argument requires.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W4229080938.c001 fails because defining divine simplicity as non-composition from more basic features does not exclude having distinct co-fundamental properties, which is exactly what the argument needs to rule out.

objection.text: In metallurgy, alloys gain strength precisely because their composite parts interact; the whole depends on its constituents, yet this dependence does not diminish the alloy’s unity or integrity. If a being’s properties were like alloy components—each reinforcing the others—then causal reliance on them would not imply fragility or contingency. The fear assumes dependence entails weakness, but interdependence can instead create stability.
objection.premise_fails_because: W4229080938.c011 fails because dependence on parts does not necessarily undermine unity or self-sufficiency.

objection.text: c001 defines divine simplicity as God not being a composite of 'more basic features.' This smuggles in a hierarchical assumption: that any genuine composition requires parts strictly ontologically prior to the whole. But c011 and c012 describe the actual threat—God depending on power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes. These are not 'more basic' than God; they are co-equal attributes or modes at the same ontological level. A composite of co-equal features (a whole constituted by aspects none of which is 'more basic' than the others) is excluded by c001's definition yet is precisely the structure c012 fears. The argument needs c001 to rule out that structure, but c001's 'more basic' qualifier makes it incapable of doing so. The premise assumes a part-whole hierarchy the rest of the argument never establishes and that the causal-dependence worry does not require.

objection.text: Consider a deity who exists through a complex interplay of its own properties, such as wisdom, power, and blessedness. In this scenario, the deity's existence is not independent of its distinct properties, but rather emerges from their dynamic relationships. This deity would still be able to act intentionally and maintain its own existence, but its properties would be inseparable from its being. For instance, its wisdom could be the causal foundation for its power, and its blessedness could be the final cause of its existence. This example shows that causal dependence on distinct properties does not necessarily undermine a deity's existence or its ability to act.
objection.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that God's existence must be independent of its distinct properties, which is not necessarily the case for a deity that exists through a complex interplay of its own properties.

objection.text: Consider City X, whose existence is grounded in two distinct facts. First, the concrete arrangement of streets, buildings, and inhabitants is a brute fact that makes the proposition 'City X exists' true in virtue of its own spatial configuration. Second, a sovereign's charter legally creates and sustains the city; the charter is a separate fact that also truth‑makes the same proposition. Truthmaker theory permits multiple, co‑existent truthmakers for a single truth without contradiction, because each truthmaker provides a different explanatory basis. Thus, a thing can exist both through a self‑grounded fact and through another fact without incoherence.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W4229080938.c009 fails because truthmaker theory allows simultaneous self‑grounding and external grounding of existence, so no contradiction arises.

objection.text: A Supreme Being is both perfectly Just and perfectly Wise. In Platonism, Justice and Wisdom are distinct, eternal, and independent universals. The Being instantiates both, making it a composite of these real, independent properties. However, the Being does not depend on Justice or Wisdom as final causes to realize its nature or achieve its existence. The Being is the locus of these properties, but the properties exist independently of the Being. The existence of a plurality of real, instantiated properties does not imply that the being is directed toward those properties for its own completion or that they act as its final cause. A being can be many-featured through the instantiation of independent universals without being causally dependent upon them. W4229080938.c012 fails because the instantiation of independent, real properties does not necessitate that those properties function as final causes or sources of causal dependence.

Consequently, God's identity is determined by the combination of these properties, making him dependent on them.

You are right that c001's 'more basic' wording is too narrow, and I will not defend it as written. Co-equal aspects can ground dependence just as well as ordered parts can, so the definition should say that God is not composed of features on which his existence depends, whether or not those features are ordered. Literature supports reading simplicity as ruling out composition in general rather than only hierarchical composition [W4232242998.a1], and [W2086535520.a1] describes simplicity as lacking any composition or metaphysical complexity, which is broader than the priority reading. The mp premise, that God is not causally dependent on his distinct properties either efficiently or as final causes, is unchanged. The revised c001 is what needs to change: it must name the dependence relation, not priority, as the thing excluded.

The objection pins the consequent of c012 on the claim that each feature is an independent target G must aim at. That is more than the argument needs. c011 frames the worry as dependence on distinct properties, and the relevant dependence is ontological: a composite's unity is secured by its constituents, so its existence and its end are answerable to them. Your proposal that G's end is a unified act whose specifications are P and W does not dissolve this.
